result:
The proposed answer of 2 is incorrect. The likely answer is 3, because nonzero triple Massey products of degree-one classes do occur on compact complex surfaces.

The error is in the "no triple Massey product can be nonzero" argument. From $f\wedge g = d\alpha$ and $g\wedge h = d\beta$, the triple Massey product is the class of $\alpha\wedge h \pm f\wedge\beta$. The proof only computes $(f\wedge g)\wedge h = d(\alpha\wedge h)$ and then asserts that the whole sum is a boundary. But $f\wedge\beta$ need not be exact, so the sum is not automatically zero. The argument does not establish vanishing.

A counterexample exists. The Kodaira–Thurston manifold, the underlying manifold of the primary Kodaira surface, is a compact complex surface. It is a nilmanifold (Heisenberg nilmanifold times $S^1$), and its Lie algebra has structure equations $de^3 = e^1\wedge e^2$ with the other generators closed. Triple Massey products of degree-one classes are nonzero there, so $N \ge 3$.

The 2-fold part of the argument is fine, since the 2-fold Massey product is the cup product. But that only shows $N\ge 2$, which the triple-product counterexample already exceeds.

VERDICT: REJECT
CONFIDENCE: 4
